title: HubSpot AEO Grader vs. Peec AI: Features, pricing, and use cases
content:
If your buyers are asking ChatGPT for vendor recommendations instead of scrolling through Google results, your brand’s visibility in AI search engines matters as much as your organic rankings … maybe more. That shift is what’s driving the rapid adoption of answer engine optimization as a discipline, and it’s why marketers are now evaluating dedicated tools to track, measure, and improve how AI platforms characterize their brand. The challenge isn’t awareness that AI is reshaping search ; it’s choosing the right tool to address it.
HubSpot AEO and Peec AI are two of the most visible platforms in this space, but they serve meaningfully different functions. One connects AI visibility insights to a CRM-driven content execution workflow. The other delivers deep monitoring and reporting infrastructure designed to feed external tools and agency dashboards.
Choosing the wrong one for your team’s stage, stack, and resources means either paying for execution capabilities you won’t use or collecting data you can’t act on. This post breaks down features, pricing, engines tracked, integrations, and actionability side by side, so you can effectively match the tool to your AI SEO workflow.
HubSpot’s AEO Grader is a free page grader that evaluates what ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini say about your brand based on their training data. No account, no credit card, no usage caps.
It’s pretty simple to get started with AEO Grader. To run your first report, you enter your:
Then, the tool runs dozens of test queries across all three AI engines, returning a composite score out of 100 with a written interpretation of your results in three to five minutes.
Peec AI , on the other hand, is a visibility monitoring platform that tracks how often your brand appears in AI-generated responses to buyer questions. The platform uses UI scraping technology to simulate real user interactions rather than querying APIs, so the responses it logs reflect what actual users see.
Now, when comparing HubSpot AEO versus Peec AI, the first thing to understand is that these are not interchangeable tools.
HubSpot’s AEO Grader provides a one-time brand visibility check across five key categories. In short, each tool serves a distinct role in your AEO stack, and the right choice depends on where your team stands today.
As I previously mentioned, HubSpot’s AEO score baseline is structured around five factors, each weighted to reflect its impact on how AI characterizes your brand.
Take a look at the chart below to see how each dimension is scored and what it measures:
The overall tone AI uses when describing your brand spanning general sentiment, contextual sentiment across topics, and the credibility of the sources shaping that characterization.
The depth and accuracy of how AI engines describe your offerings, capabilities, and differentiators.
Whether AI engines reliably identify, name, and categorize your brand when responding to relevant queries.
How frequently your brand appears in AI responses relative to competitors in the same category.
Your perceived competitive positioning and market standing within AI-generated answers.
Overall, Sentiment Analysis carries the most weight among these areas because it measures how AI characterizes your brand.
This article positions HubSpot AEO as the primary product comparison, and AEO Grader as the low-friction entry point.
Here’s why: AEO Grader answers, “How does AI represent my brand right now?” HubSpot AEO answers, “How is that changing, and what should I do about it?”
This comparison evaluates features, pricing, engines tracked, prompts, integrations, and actionability, so here’s what Peec AI delivers:
The right tool depends on your stage of AEO maturity and what you intend to do with the data.
Here’s a practical decision framework to utilize when it’s time to make a choice:
Establishes a scored baseline across five categories in under five minutes — zero commitment required.
You need continuous tracking and competitor benchmarking.
Both offer ongoing monitoring. HubSpot AEO includes CRM-connected recommendations; Peec AI offers deeper multi-engine reporting.
You need to act on visibility gaps (not just measure them).
HubSpot AEO surfaces what to fix. Marketing Hub is where you build and publish the content that fixes it.
You manage multiple client brands and need scaled reporting.
Multi-project accounts, agency credit systems, white-label dashboards, and per-project engine selection.
You’re building a business case for leadership buy-in.
A composite score out of 100 with a written interpretation is significantly more communicable than paid-tool dashboards.
Pro tip: If you’re unsure whether continuous monitoring is worth the investment, I recommend starting with the AEO Grader. A low Sentiment or Share of Voice score signals that monitoring (and execution) should follow quickly.
A strong baseline may mean the priority is maintaining visibility rather than rebuilding it. Either way, HubSpot’s brand visibility report with AEO Grader gives you a concrete data point to bring into the conversation rather than a theoretical pitch.
To help you make a confident decision, I’ve compared the following:
When choosing between AEO tools, the feature list matters far less than what you can actually do with the data.
Here’s a transparent breakdown of how HubSpot AEO and Peec AI stack up across the capabilities that shape your day-to-day workflow:
HubSpot AEO tracks brand visibility across three answer engines:
All three are included on every plan with no add-on fees.
HubSpot’s broader web analytics also recognizes AI referral clicks from Copilot, Claude, and Meta AI inside its “AI Referrals” traffic source, so while prompt-level tracking covers three engines, your attribution picture extends further.
Alternatively, Peec AI tracks ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews on every plan, with Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Grok available as paid add-ons. Every self-serve plan limits engine selection to three out of the seven available options (a constraint that holds from the Starter through the Advanced tier).
Pro tip: If Gemini is a priority engine for your audience, note the difference. HubSpot AEO includes Gemini across all plans. With Peec AI, Gemini is an add-on, and choosing it means dropping one of your three default engines unless you pay extra.
No matter what the feature lists say, prompt tracking is the core of both platforms. However, how prompts are generated, capped, and connected to your business context varies significantly between HubSpot AEO and Peec AI.
HubSpot AEO uses your Smart CRM data (i.e., products, ICPs, competitor names, and deal stages) to auto-generate prompt suggestions tailored to your actual business. Then, the CRM connects contact and company records directly to AEO prompt recommendations, so tracking starts with buyer-relevant queries from day one rather than generic industry templates.
I’ll get into pricing for both tools in more detail later on, but for now, here’s a brief look at HubSpot AEO pricing as it relates to prompt caps:
Peec AI suggests prompts based on search intent signals and lets teams organize them by persona, funnel stage, or topic tags.
Here’s a brief look at Peec AI pricing as it relates to prompt caps:
Basically, Peec AI offers more raw prompt volume at each tier. HubSpot AEO offers fewer prompts but connects them directly to your CRM context and content execution workflows, which is a considerable trade-off between breadth and depth of integration.
Both platforms surface which domains and pages are cited in AI-generated responses, but the depth and how you use those insights differ.
HubSpot AEO connects visibility insights to content and campaign execution workflows. Its citation analysis breaks down sources by the following types:
When a gap appears, HubSpot AEO surfaces prioritized recommendations and connects them directly to HubSpot’s Marketing Hub content tools, so your team can create or update the content that closes that gap without leaving the platform. (Also, Marketing Hub supports content and campaign execution after AI visibility insights are identified. The blog post, landing page, or LinkedIn post all get built where the data lives.)
Conversely, Peec AI focuses on AI visibility monitoring and reporting through its Sources feature, which shows the exact URLs that AI engines cite for each prompt. These cited URLs are categorized by:
Its Gap Analysis scores sources that frequently cite competitors but not you, giving teams a prioritized target list for digital PR and authority-building outreach.
HubSpot AEO runs every tracked prompt daily across all three engines on a 24-hour refresh cycle. Data refreshes automatically. No manual runs required.
Now, Peec AI also tracks daily on all paid plans. But because Peec uses UI scraping technology rather than API calls, responses reflect what real users see in each engine’s interface, which can surface formatting and citation differences that API-based tools miss.
Nevertheless, both platforms deliver daily data, so the update cadence is effectively equivalent.
This is where the platforms diverge most sharply, and where the HubSpot AEO or Peec AI choice often comes down to your team’s reporting stack.
To save you the stress of going back and forth between product pages, here’s a brief, quick hit guide to export, reporting, and integration capabilities for both tools:
HubSpot AEO surfaces visibility changes through its dashboard, trend views, and recommendation updates inside Marketing Hub.
While not a standalone alerting system, the prioritized recommendations act as a functional alert layer; when visibility drops or a competitor gains share of voice, a new recommendation appears with a specific action attached.
Now, Peec AI, on the other hand, is a little different. It offers more configurable alerting through its MCP integration. Teams can wire up daily sentiment checks that trigger Slack or email alerts when a brand’s sentiment drops below a defined threshold, including the exact AI responses that caused the shift. (This is available on all of its paid plans.)
If your team started with the free AEO Grader , you already have a baseline score across the following AI search dimensions:
Peec AI does not offer a free baseline diagnostic. Teams evaluating Peec start with a paid subscription from day one.
Here’s the (short) scoop on what each platform does best: HubSpot AEO is the right choice when your priority is connecting AI visibility data to content execution and pipeline reporting in a single platform. However, Peec AI is the strongest choice when your priority is scaled monitoring, external reporting, and multi-engine analytics.
Use this chart to help assess which strengths matter most for your team:
Pro tip: These tools aren’t mutually exclusive. Some teams run HubSpot AEO for CRM-connected execution and Peec AI for expanded engine coverage and client reporting, using each where it’s strongest rather than forcing one platform to do everything.
Pricing is where the HubSpot AEO versus Peec AI comparison gets concrete.
Both platforms use prompt-based billing, but they structure costs, trials, seats, and scaling very differently, and those differences have real implications depending on whether you’re an SMB testing AEO for the first time, a mid-market team embedding it into an existing CRM workflow, or an agency managing ten client brands.
In this section, I’ll provide a transparent, no BS breakdown that’ll help you make a decision grounded in your budget, team size, and reporting needs.
The article positions HubSpot AEO as the primary product comparison and AEO Grader as the low-friction entry point, and the pricing structure reflects that philosophy.
HubSpot AEO offers two free entry paths before any spend:
After the trial, HubSpot AEO’s standalone plan is $50/month ($45/month on annual billing). That includes 25 prompts tracked daily across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, with up to 2,500 answers per month. No additional HubSpot subscription is required.
Peec AI does not offer a free tier or a free baseline diagnostic. Instead, it offers:
Pro tip: HubSpot AEO is included at no additional cost with Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise. If your team is already on either plan, AEO is already available; there’s no reason not to activate it immediately.
Prompt limits are the single biggest cost lever in both platforms, but they scale differently.
All of this said, the trade-off is clear: Peec AI offers more prompt volume at each tier. HubSpot AEO offers fewer prompts but connects each one to CRM context and an execution workflow. But this doesn’t mean that one tool is better than the other.
If prompt volume is your primary constraint, Peec scales further at comparable price points. If prompt quality and actionability matter more, HubSpot AEO’s CRM-generated suggestions reduce the guesswork.
HubSpot AEO’s seat model depends on how you access it. The standalone $50/month plan offers open dashboard access. Marketing Hub Professional includes 3 core seats (additional seats at $45/month each); Enterprise includes 5 (additional at $75/month each).
View-only seats are free on both Marketing Hub plans, which is useful for stakeholders who need visibility into AEO data without editing permissions.
However, Peec AI includes unlimited seats across all paid plans, from Starter to Enterprise. This is a meaningful procurement advantage for larger teams and agencies where per-seat pricing creates budget friction.
HubSpot AEO includes ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity on every plan with no add-on fees and no engine-selection constraints. HubSpot’s broader web analytics separately tracks AI referral traffic from Copilot, Claude, and Meta AI.
But each self-serve plan limits selection to three. Additional engines cost €20–30/month each as add-ons. Claude is available only on the custom-priced Enterprise plan. Both platforms support multi-language and multi-region tracking at no extra prompt cost.
HubSpot AEO keeps reporting native to the HubSpot ecosystem. AEO data appears alongside:
The best part? No manual stitching is required. Marketing Hub also supports content and campaign execution after AI visibility insights are identified, so the path from insight to published content stays inside one platform.
By contrast, Peec AI has a more open export architecture. CSV exports are included on all plans. Looker Studio connectivity arrives on Advanced ($495/month). API access is Enterprise-only.
Additionally, MCP integration (for automated Slack alerts, n8n/Make workflows, and Claude-powered reports) is included on all paid plans at no extra cost, which is a notable differentiator for teams building custom reporting pipelines.
HubSpot AEO surfaces visibility shifts through its recommendation engine inside Marketing Hub. When a competitor gains share of voice or your visibility on a key prompt drops, a new recommendation appears with a specific next action attached.
Peec AI offers more configurable alerting via its MCP integration. Teams can set sentiment thresholds that trigger Slack or email notifications when a brand’s score drops below a defined level, including the exact AI responses that caused the shift.
Mid-market Teams (10 to 50 Marketers, Existing HubSpot Stack)
Agency Teams (Multiple Client Brands, External Reporting Needs)
$50/month standalone with free trial and free Grader baseline
Requires Marketing Hub Enterprise or expansion packs
Credit pooling across projects, agency-tier pricing
CSV, Looker Studio, API (Enterprise), MCP (all plans)
Here’s the thing: Monitoring AI visibility is only useful if you can do something with what you find.
This is the single biggest differentiator in the HubSpot AEO versus Peec AI comparison, and where the two platforms diverge most clearly.
Understanding the AEO workflow as a whole will help you determine which one best fits your team. Below, I’ve provided an overview of how it functions.
Regardless of which platform you choose, AI visibility tools follow a common operational loop. The difference between tools is how many steps of this loop they handle natively versus how many require external resources.
Peec AI delivers strong analytics but stops at the execution boundary by design. The platform tells you where your brand is underperforming and which sources competitors are leveraging, then expects your team to handle the content and authority-building work independently.
Here’s the honest 411 on where Peec AI’s workflow excels:
AI citation tracking tools only deliver value if your team actually uses them and keeps using them after the first week.
In the HubSpot AEO versus Peec AI comparison, both platforms score well on interface design and initial accessibility, but they diverge on:
In the sections below, I’ve outlined what to expect from each.
HubSpot AEO is designed for fast onboarding with minimal technical expertise required. The onboarding flow works like this:
Peec AI also earns high marks for interface clarity and fast activation. Basic setup involves:
The dashboard shows initial AI visibility scores, broken down by engine, within a few minutes of completing configuration. Reviewers routinely describe understanding the full product within about 30 minutes.
The key difference: HubSpot AEO’s onboarding is guided by your CRM data , which reduces the upfront decisions a marketer needs to make. Peec AI’s onboarding is clean and fast, but prompt selection relies either on the user’s knowledge of their buyer landscape or on Peec’s intent-based suggestions.
Pro tip: Both tools have minimal learning curves. Neither requires technical expertise to set up, configure, or interpret results — a meaningful advantage over enterprise-grade platforms that require dedicated implementation cycles.
Getting value from an AEO tool often depends on whether you can share the findings with people who don’t live in dashboards. Both platforms address this, but with different strengths.
HubSpot AEO presents data in a centralized dashboard with three headline metrics:
The plain-language format makes outputs immediately shareable. Because AEO data lives inside Marketing Hub alongside campaign metrics and pipeline reporting, it’s already in the system where most stakeholders consume performance data.
Peec AI offers a clean, information-dense dashboard that provides visibility into:
All of which is organized logically on the landing screen. For external reporting, Peec supports CSV exports on all plans, Looker Studio connectivity on Advanced plans and above, and MCP-powered automated summaries that can be pushed to Slack or email.
AEO is a new discipline. Many marketers are encountering it for the first time, and the tool they choose needs to meet them where they are — not assume they already understand prompt strategy, citation analysis, or share-of-voice benchmarking.
HubSpot AEO addresses this by guiding users from insight to action without requiring AEO expertise. The Recommendations tab surfaces prioritized next steps (e.g., “create a blog post on [topic],” “update [existing page],” “publish a LinkedIn post on [theme]” ), with the reasoning behind each recommendation visible.
Peec AI keeps the interface accessible while offering more analytical depth. Prompt analytics, source analysis, and competitor benchmarking are all navigable without technical expertise. Plus, Peec’s Actions feature (in beta) surfaces recommended next steps, such as improving review site profiles, joining relevant discussions, or investing in digital PR. The recommendations are directional rather than one-click-executable, which works well for teams that already have a content production process in place.
Pro tip: HubSpot Academy also offers a free AEO Certification Course (Implementing AEO) , which provides structured training for teams new to the discipline. For organizations where AEO knowledge is concentrated in one person, that shared learning resource reduces key-person risk.
The right tool isn’t just the one with the best features. In fact, it’s the one your team will consistently use given your current resources.
Here’s how each platform fits across common team profiles.
These teams need fast time-to-value with the fewest possible moving parts. The AEO Grader → free trial → $50/month standalone path lets a solo marketer go from first baseline to daily tracking without coordinating across tools.
Peec AI’s clean interface works well here too, but the lack of built-in execution means the solo marketer needs a separate CMS, content editor, and publishing workflow — adding steps that compound when resources are limited.
Mid-market Team (5 to 15 Marketers, Dedicated Content and SEO Roles)
These teams typically have the headcount to act on insights but need the AI search performance tools to fit into an existing workflow rather than creating a new one. If the team already lives in HubSpot, activating AEO inside Marketing Hub is zero-friction adoption — the data appears where the team already works.
If the team’s content stack is outside HubSpot (WordPress, Webflow, Contentful), Peec AI’s standalone monitoring can be integrated without requiring a platform migration. The credit system also scales more naturally when tracking multiple product lines or regions.
Best for HubSpot-native mid-market teams: HubSpot AEO.
Best for mid-market teams with non-HubSpot content stacks: Peec AI.
Agencies need two things from AEO visibility tools: scalable multi-client management and client-facing reporting that doesn’t require hours of manual formatting.
Peec AI focuses on AI visibility monitoring and reporting, with a purpose-built agency tier that includes:
That infrastructure maps directly to how agencies operate. HubSpot AEO requires a separate account purchase for each client ($50/month each), with no cross-brand dashboard, which adds operational friction at scale.
Enterprise Teams (50+ Marketers, RevOps Integration Needs)
Enterprise teams care about governance, attribution, and CRM connectivity. Marketing Hub Enterprise includes HubSpot AEO with 50 prompts, and the native Smart CRM integration means AEO data feeds directly into:
But keep in mind, connecting that data to the pipeline and attribution requires manual integration work.
Best for CRM-connected enterprise workflows: HubSpot AEO.
Best for enterprise teams needing 7+ engine coverage: Peec AI.
The integration architecture of your AEO tool determines how easily visibility data moves into the systems where your team actually works, and how much manual effort sits between an insight and an action.
In the HubSpot AEO versus Peec AI comparison, the two platforms take fundamentally different approaches: HubSpot AEO is built into a connected CRM and marketing platform; Peec AI is built to export data into whatever stack you already run.
My point? Both tools are valid. Choosing the right AEO tool depends on where your team is based and what you plan to do with the data.
HubSpot AEO is natively embedded inside the HubSpot platform. AEO data sits alongside the following core components:
This information doesn’t live in a separate tab, login, or dashboard. It’s naturally embedded, and that native integration creates three practical advantages for faster insight-to-execution:
HubSpot’s broader integration ecosystem includes 2,200+ apps in its marketplace and a data-versioned API that supports custom data connections, webhooks, and workflow automation
This ensures your AEO data can reach external systems when needed, even though the primary workflow stays within the platform.
Peec AI takes an open-architecture approach. Rather than building execution or CMS tools into the platform, Peec builds the connectors that let teams pipe visibility data into whatever systems they prefer.
Here’s a closer look at Peec AI’s integration capabilities by tier:
Peec AI is purpose-built to feed data outward into your CMS, BI tools, and reporting dashboards rather than to house an execution workflow internally.
That makes it a natural fit for teams whose content production, publishing, and reporting already live in external systems like WordPress, Webflow, Looker, or Tableau.
Not every team needs CRM-connected AEO from day one. That said, connect HubSpot AEO to your CRM when:
Integration value depends on the data volume and coverage your plan provides.
Here’s how each platform scales across the dimensions that matter most.
Every section above has compared features, pricing, workflows, and integrations. This section makes the decision simple.
If you’ve read the full comparison, you already know the details. If you’ve skipped ahead, this section tells you which tool fits your team; read on for the simplified verdict.
Basically, pick HubSpot AEO when your priority is acting on AI visibility data, not just collecting it.
If you’re still not convinced, here are the scenarios where it’s the clear fit:
I’ve already mentioned that Peec AI is primarily an AI visibility monitoring and reporting tool. That monitoring-first architecture is the right choice when your team needs analytics depth, external reporting infrastructure, or scaled multi-client management without requiring a specific execution platform.
That said, I recommend choosing Peec AI based on the following use cases:
Global and multi-brand organizations face distinct constraints when choosing between HubSpot AEO and Peec AI. Neither platform has an obvious advantage across every scenario.
To help you better evaluate which tool would be the best investment for your organization, I’ve overviewed how each platform handles multi-region and multi-brand use cases below:
Both platforms support multi-language and multi-region prompt tracking at no extra prompt cost. Peec AI gates country coverage by tier: Starter supports 1 country per project, Pro supports 3, and Advanced expands to multi-country.
HubSpot AEO includes multi-region tracking on all plans without per-country restrictions. For teams tracking the same brand across 5+ markets, it avoids the tier-gating constraint. However, for teams running separate projects per region (common in agencies), Peec AI’s multi-project structure with per-project country settings may be more operationally natural.
HubSpot offers two architectural paths for multi-brand organizations: HubSpot Brands (formerly Business Units), an add-on for Marketing Hub Enterprise that lets you manage multiple brands from a single account with separate branding, marketing assets, and reporting — while sharing a centralized CRM; or multiple separate accounts connected through multi-account management.
HubSpot AEO currently operates as a single-brand, single-account tool. Multi-brand organizations on HubSpot Enterprise can run AEO within their primary account and use the Brands infrastructure to manage brand-specific content execution. However, organizations with fully separate accounts would need AEO to be activated per account.
Peec AI handles multi-brand natively through its project structure. Each project can track a different:
Agency plans pool credits across all projects, and brand plans offer up to 5 projects on the Advanced plan. But, for organizations with a portfolio of brands that operate independently, Peec AI’s per-project architecture avoids the account-level constraints that HubSpot’s single-brand AEO tool currently imposes.
Still not sure what to choose? Take a look at the chart I created below to match your scenario to the right platform:
Requires Pro ($245/mo) for 3 countries, or Advanced for more
Separate accounts, $50/mo each, no consolidated view
Advanced (5 projects) or agency tiers with credit pooling
For teams that choose HubSpot AEO, understanding how the tool scales within the broader platform helps you plan for growth rather than hitting unexpected limits.
Here’s what I recommend to scale your AEO program without hitting unexpected limits:
Pro tip: The comparison evaluates features, pricing, engines tracked, prompts, integrations, and actionability, but the single most predictive factor in AEO tool success is whether your team will actually execute on the insights consistently.
A tool embedded in your existing workflow will see higher adoption than one that requires a separate login and a manual data transfer. If your team works in HubSpot, that means HubSpot AEO. If your team works in a different stack, that means Peec AI. Match the tool to the workflow, not the other way around.
Before choosing between HubSpot AEO, Peec AI, or any other AI visibility tool, you need a number.
Not a dashboard, not a trial, not a sales call. A real, tangible number. Or, even better, a scored baseline that tells you exactly how AI engines characterize your brand right now.
HubSpot’s AEO Grader provides a one-time brand visibility check across five scoring layers. The entire process takes under five minutes with no account, no credit card, and no usage caps.
Your composite score is the weighted sum of the five AEO performance areas.
Here’s what each one actually tells you and what a low score in that area means for your next steps.
Pro tip: Use HubSpot’s free AI Search Guide to better translate what “AI visibility” means into specific, measurable concepts, making it the clearest way to explain AEO to a CMO, board member, or cross-functional stakeholder who’s never encountered the category.
Most teams don’t. But it depends on what you’re optimizing for.
HubSpot AEO connects visibility insights to content and campaign execution workflows, making it the stronger choice when your team needs to act on gaps inside a CRM-connected platform. Peec AI is the better fit if your primary need is analytics depth, external BI exports, or scaled multi-client management.
That said, some teams do run both, and there is (surprisingly) a practical case for it:
Running both only makes sense if you have the budget ($50/month + $95/month minimum) and the team capacity to use two dashboards consistently.
TL;DR — If you’re choosing one, match the tool to the workflow your team will actually execute.
Yes. HubSpot AEO is available as a standalone product at $50/month ($45/month on annual billing) with no additional HubSpot subscription required. The standalone plan includes:
Here’s a more in-depth breakdown of how the access tiers scale:
The standalone plan is a fully functional product. The difference with HubSpot’s Marketing Hub is the depth of CRM context it provides.
In short, Marketing Hub supports content and campaign execution after AI-generated insights are identified, so recommendations connect to richer buyer data and a broader content toolset. (But $50/month standalone is a legitimate starting point, and many teams begin there before upgrading.)
Peec AI is the stronger fit for most agency workflows. The platform’s agency tiers are purpose-built for multi-client operations with credit pooling across projects, unlimited seats, per-project engine selection, and pitch workspaces for winning new business.
Here’s a brief look at how Peec AI’s agency plans to scale:
Agencies also get CSV exports on all plans, Looker Studio connectivity for client dashboards (where available by tier), and an Agency Partner Program with directory listing, co-branded initiatives, and coaching resources.
AEO Grader provides a one-time brand visibility check across five brand signals, each pointing to a different type of improvement.

After implementing changes, rerun the AEO diagnostic monthly to track progress. Over time, the five core AEO pillars from your initial baseline become the KPIs you measure against.
For B2B audiences in 2026, the three engines that matter most are ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini — which are the three engines HubSpot AEO tracks on every plan. Here’s why each matters and where the HubSpot AEO vs Peec AI engine coverage differences become relevant.
The bottom line for B2B teams? ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini cover the highest-volume B2B buyer touchpoints, and both platforms track all three. The engine coverage “debate” in the HubSpot AEO or Peec AI conversation only becomes decisive when your audience relies heavily on Copilot, Claude, or Google AI Mode, in which case Peec AI’s broader engine selection offers more flexibility, but at a higher price point.
Alright, reader. We’ve come to an end on this one, and I’ve got one last thing to say: Choosing HubSpot AEO or Peec AI isn’t a matter of which tool is objectively better. Instead, it’s a matter of which one fits how your team already works.
If your content workflows, campaign management, and buyer data live in HubSpot, HubSpot AEO turns AI-generated insights into published content without adding a new platform to your stack. If your execution tools live elsewhere and your primary need is scaled monitoring, external reporting, or multi-client management, Peec AI delivers the analytics depth and export infrastructure to feed the systems you already run.
The entire comparison — features, pricing, engines, integrations, actionability — points back to that single question: Where does your team do its best work?
AI visibility is measurable, scoreable, and improvable. The tools exist. The frameworks exist. What separates the teams that gain ground from those that keep auditing is whether they pick a tool that fits their workflow and actually use it.

title: 5 Semrush AI visibility alternatives worth testing
content:
For many, Semrush is the gold standard for tracking traditional SERP rankings, and the tool has recently added AI visibility features to its suite. However, there are plenty of Semrush AI visibility alternatives on the market worth exploring.
This guide compares eight alternatives — including HubSpot AEO — to help SEO leaders, content marketers, demand gen managers, and RevOps teams evaluate the right fit for their stack, their reporting needs, and their budget.
AI search visibility is a brand’s presence inside AI-generated answers — the citations, summaries, and recommendations that AI engines like ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews , and Gemini produce in response to user queries.
Traditional rank tracking measures where a webpage appears in a list of blue links. AI search visibility measures whether a brand’s content is retrieved, synthesized, and surfaced as a trusted source inside a generated response.
The core difference is structure. In traditional search, ranking depends heavily on backlinks, domain authority, and keyword alignment. In AI search, visibility depends on whether an AI search engine can confidently interpret, extract, and attribute a brand’s content.
A page can hold a strong position in Google’s organic results and still be absent from AI-generated answers simply because AI systems prioritize clarity, entity authority, and cross-platform consistency over ranking signals alone.
Featured Resource: I Ran 100s of Queries to Find Out if AI Chatbots Are Better Than Search Engines
Three metrics define AI search visibility in practice.
Together, these three metrics provide more complete insight into AI search visibility than any single metric alone. A brand can have high citation frequency but poor sentiment, or low share of voice but strong positioning in the citations it does earn. Understanding all three is what makes AI visibility measurement actionable.
Semrush added AI visibility tracking as an extension of its existing SEO suite, layering AI Overview monitoring, limited citation insights, and keyword data for AI‑influenced queries in addition to its traditional tooling. For teams already working inside Semrush for technical SEO, backlinks, and competitive research, this reduces tool switching and keeps everything in a single workspace.
Its AI visibility features lean heavily toward Google AI Overviews, Gemini, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and traditional search integrations. Semrush’s AI visibility features do not cover emerging assistants like Meta AI, Copilot, or Yahoo Scout. This is a gap for teams that need broader cross‑engine visibility.
And for organizations not already standardized on Semrush, pricing remains one of the biggest barriers to adopting its AI layer.
HubSpot AEO (Answer Engine Optimization) is built specifically to track and improve brand visibility inside AI-generated answers. Where most SEO tools treat AI visibility as an add-on, HubSpot AEO is designed around it. The tool connects citation data, share of voice, and competitor comparisons directly to the CRM context and content tools teams already use.
What makes it different: HubSpot AEO connects visibility data to Marketing Hub ‘s campaign reporting and Smart CRM’ s pipeline and revenue attribution. That means a demand gen team can see not just where the brand appears in AI answers, but whether those AI-influenced touchpoints are converting into contacts, deals, and pipeline.
The AEO Grader — HubSpot’s free baseline tool — provides teams with a benchmark before committing to a full platform. It scores AI visibility across major engines and surfaces where competitors are being cited instead. Smart CRM integration is the piece that closes the attribution loop for RevOps teams who need to tie AI visibility data to revenue reporting.
What I like: The combination of the AEO Grader for baselining and Marketing Hub for reporting makes HubSpot AEO the most complete option for teams who’ve already felt the pain of trying to connect AI visibility data to actual business outcomes.
What the experts say : Peter Baraník , founder of ColorWee and a digital marketer, told me, “I super love this tool because it gives you four things out of the box: a visibility score, prompt tracking, citation analysis, and prioritized recommendations, with the main dashboard showing how your brand trends over time across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. The setup is straightforward, the data can be interpreted without an SEO team, and at only $50 per month, it doesn’t require a big budget commitment to try.”
He added, “One limitation is that it only includes three platforms, so if you care about Claude, Grok, or Google AI Mode, there will be gaps.”
Best for: Marketing, demand gen, and RevOps teams who need AI visibility data connected to CRM reporting and pipeline impact.
Pro tip: Start with the AEO Grader to establish your baseline before comparing against competitors. The benchmark data gives your RevOps team a defensible starting point for measuring progress.
LLM Pulse is a dedicated AI visibility platform focused on citation analysis, sentiment tracking, and query fan-out research across major AI models. The platform shows actual AI responses — not just aggregated scores — which makes it useful for teams who want to audit what AI engines are literally saying about their brand.
What I like: LLM Pulse is one of the few tools that surface query fan-out data, which shows the full range of prompts AI engines use to retrieve content on a topic. That helps design an AI search content strategy, not just monitoring.
What the experts say: Doug Darroch , Managing Director at Renaissance Digital Marketing, said, “LLM Pulse stands out because of its white-label reporting. Beyond basic mention tracking, it covers citation analysis, sentiment, query fan-out, and prompt research across the major models, and it shows you the actual AI responses. The main limitation is that the optimization step leans on AI-generated recommendations rather than built-in content production, so you are still the one doing the strategic execution.”
Best for: Agencies managing AI visibility for multiple clients, and brands that want to see the actual AI responses pulling their content.
BrightEdge is an enterprise SEO platform that has expanded into AI search tracking, offering features such as AI Overview monitoring, content recommendations, and large-scale keyword analysis.
What I like: BrightEdge’s integration of AI visibility into a broader enterprise AI SEO workflow reduces the need to manage separate platforms for teams with large content operations.
What the experts say: Baraník has an honest opinion about BrightEdge. He told me, “BrightEdge can be useful if your problem is enterprise SEO workflow, but it’s not enough if your problem is specifically AI search visibility, because buyers are no longer just clicking on ranked pages. They’re using ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, and Perplexity to summarize markets for them. The data is impressive, but the platform is geared toward large teams with dedicated SEO resources, and the pricing reflects that. If you are a one-man band or a small brand, it’s more tools than you need.”
Best for: Enterprise SEO teams with existing BrightEdge contracts who want to extend visibility tracking into AI Overviews without switching platforms.
Authoritas measures how visible your brand is across AI search experiences. The tool tracks which entities, products, and competitors appear in AI answers and how often.
What I like: Authoritas gives marketers a clear, structured view of how my brand actually appears in AI search without the guesswork.
What the experts say: Raúl Menoyo , Founder of Citora, uses a variety of Semrush AI visibility alternatives each day. Here’s what he had to say about Authoritas: “The feature I genuinely rely on is URL-level AI Overview tracking, which tells me which exact pages Google is citing instead of handing me one vague visibility score. Its blind spot is the standalone assistants. It’s strong on Google and thin on ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity, so I have to pair it with something else when a client cares about those.”
Best for: SEO teams focused primarily on Google AI Overviews who need page-level citation data to prioritize content updates.
Advanced Web Ranking tracks how your brand appears across AI search results, showing which competitors are being surfaced and how your visibility shifts over time.
What I like: Advanced Web Ranking’s historical data makes it easy to demonstrate progress over time. It’s useful for reporting to stakeholders who want to see trend lines, not just current snapshots.
What the experts say: Manpreet Kaur, SEO Specialist, said, “This tool has become one of my go-to tools when it comes to keyword tracking and SEO reporting. The thing I like about it is the opportunity to track ranking positions across various locations, devices, and search engines, providing historical trend information along the way. For SEO professionals who need reliable tools for tracking their visibility and getting comprehensive reporting data, Advanced Web Ranking works great.”
Best for: SEO teams managing multi-location or multi-market visibility who need reliable historical tracking alongside AI search data.
The best AI visibility tool is the one that aligns with where your buyers search, how your team reports, and whether visibility data needs to connect to revenue workflows. Here are the questions to consider when deciding whether to subscribe to an AI visibility tool.
Start with buyer behavior. If most research happens in Google AI Overviews, tools with strong Google coverage — like Authoritas or BrightEdge — will give you the clearest signal.
If your audience is using ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Gemini, cross‑assistant tracking becomes essential. HubSpot AEO and LLM Pulse both monitor multiple major assistants, making them better fits for teams that need visibility beyond Google.
Your “best” tool depends on the workflow you’re optimizing for.
If you need visibility data tied directly to pipeline, attribution, and CRM context, HubSpot AEO is the most complete option because it connects natively to Smart CRM and Marketing Hub.
If you’re producing client‑ready or agency‑style deliverables, LLM Pulse stands out with flexible, white‑label reporting.
If you need deeper insight into how Google AI Overviews cite your content, Authoritas offers more granular detail than most alternatives.
HubSpot AEO and LLM Pulse both track visibility across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. Advanced Web Ranking and Authoritas offer stronger traditional search coverage, with varying levels of AI assistant integration.
Pro tip: Because coverage changes quickly, always confirm current engine support with the vendor before committing.
Most standalone AI visibility tools require manual exports to bring citation data into CRM reporting. HubSpot AEO is the only tool that removes that friction. Visibility data appears alongside CRM records, campaign performance, and pipeline metrics without additional integration work.
I’ve talked to several marketers about the future of SEO . For teams looking to launch their AI visibility strategy, the first thing I tell them is to define success before measuring or changing any part of the content marketing strategy, which gives the pilot enough runway to produce meaningful data. Here’s the six-step structure I recommend.
Start with 10 to 15 queries that reflect how your buyers actually research in AI engines. Not internal keyword lists, but real buyer questions at evaluation and decision stages. Queries like:
Run your target queries manually across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini before setting up any tracking tool. Document citation frequency, competitor mentions, and how your brand is described. This baseline is your starting point, and it makes the first reporting cycle more meaningful.
Use HubSpot’s AEO Grader for a structured benchmark. The Grader scores your visibility across major AI engines and identifies where competitors are appearing instead of you.
Use the criteria in the previous section to choose the right tool for your team. If you’re managing CRM-connected reporting, start with HubSpot AEO. If you need white-label deliverables, evaluate LLM Pulse. If Google AI Overviews are your primary surface, Authoritas is worth testing.
AI visibility gaps that are content gaps are usually places where your brand’s expertise on a topic isn’t clear, well-structured, or up to date enough for AI engines to confidently retrieve. Review your top-performing pages against your baseline citation data. Pages that rank well in traditional search but appear infrequently in AI answers often need structural improvements:
At the end of your first reporting cycle (4 to 8 weeks is a reasonable starting window), measure four things.
This step is where most AI visibility pilots stall. Citation data without revenue attribution doesn’t move budget conversations.
HubSpot AEO’s connection to Smart CRM and Marketing Hub makes this step possible within the platform. If you’re using a standalone tool, build a manual bridge: tag contacts by AI-influenced touchpoints and track them through the pipeline in your CRM.
Yes, you can run AI visibility tracking alongside Semrush rather than replacing it. Most teams keep Semrush for traditional SEO workflows — technical audits, backlink analysis, keyword tracking — and layer a dedicated AI visibility tool like HubSpot AEO on top for citation monitoring, share of voice, and AI engine coverage. The two workflows operate independently, so there’s no technical conflict.
Rank tracking measures where a webpage appears in search results, typically by position, keyword, and search engine. AI visibility measures whether and how a brand appears inside AI‑generated answers, which don’t have traditional ranked positions. Instead of “position one versus position five,” AI visibility tracks citation frequency (how often a brand is mentioned), share of voice (how often a brand appears relative to competitors), and sentiment (how AI engines describe the brand).
Yes, HubSpot’s AEO Grader is a free tool that scores brand visibility across major AI engines and surfaces gaps in competitors. Manual prompt testing — running target-buyer queries across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini and documenting the results — is also a zero‑cost baseline approach. Both are solid starting points before committing to a paid platform. The limitation is scale: free options don’t support ongoing monitoring or automated reporting, so for regular tracking and stakeholder updates, a paid tool is more practical.
Connecting AI visibility to revenue requires a bridge between citation data and CRM records. The most direct path is to use a platform that natively integrates visibility tracking with CRM. HubSpot AEO connects to Smart CRM and Marketing Hub, so AI‑influenced touchpoints can be tied to contacts, deals, and pipeline without manual export. If you’re using a standalone AI visibility tool, the manual approach involves tagging contacts by AI‑influenced discovery sources and tracking their conversion path in the CRM. The key is defining AI‑influenced touchpoints before the pilot starts, so attribution logic is in place once the data begins flowing.
For most marketing teams, AI search visibility is a current reporting gap. And my experience working with brands on AI search strategy consistently points to the same conclusion: citation data is only as useful as the reporting infrastructure around it.
Teams that can connect AI visibility to revenue conversations are the ones that secure ongoing investment in the channel. HubSpot AEO’s integration with Smart CRM and Marketing Hub is the most complete solution I’ve seen for closing that loop, and the AEO Grader gives teams a free, structured starting point before committing to any platform.
If your team is evaluating Semrush AI visibility alternatives, start with the AEO Grader for a baseline, define your target queries and success metrics before the pilot launches, and prioritize the tool that makes visibility data actionable inside the workflows you already use.

title: What Top Stories Inside AI Overviews Means For Publishers And Brands In 2026 And Beyond via @sejournal, @gregjarboe
content:
John Shehata, CEO of NewzDash, found something in July that a lot of publishers threatening to block Google’s AI don’t realize is already happening underneath them. Google has started folding entire Top Stories carousels directly inside AI Overviews , and the robots.txt directive most publishers reach for first does nothing to stop it.
Shehata posted on LinkedIn that nearly one in six U.S. trending news queries now place Top Stories inside AI Overviews, and followed it with a full data breakdown on the NewzDash SEO for News blog .
The topic he is describing is not new in kind, but it is new in mechanism. In 2006, John and I spoke on a panel about “Vertical Creep Into Regular Search Results” at the Search Engine Strategies New York conference. We discussed how Google was quietly pulling what appeared in Google News into its main web results before Universal Search formally arrived. Danny Sullivan called that May 2007 rollout the most radical change Google had ever shipped to its results, blending video, images, books, and news into a single ranked list instead of 10 blue links. Google’s own announcement framed it the same way, describing a shift toward one integrated set of results rather than separate verticals users had to hunt through individually.
Nineteen years later, Google is doing it again. This time the destination isn’t a blended results page. It’s an AI-generated answer.
According to NewzDash’s tracking, among trending news queries where Google displays Top Stories at all, 15.5% in the U.S. and 17.46% in the UK now show that carousel embedded inside the AI Overview rather than as its own standalone module below it. Entertainment queries lead both countries, clearing 35% in the U.S. and 31.5% in the UK. World News hits nearly 32% in the U.S. Health and Science queries barely register. Shehata’s data also shows the two placements are mutually exclusive. When Top Stories lives inside the AI Overview, Google is not also running a separate carousel further down the page for the same query.
That distinction matters more than it sounds like it should, because it reframes the entire opt-out conversation publishers have been having since AI Overviews launched.
Most publishers who want out point their robots.txt at Google-Extended and consider the matter settled. It isn’t. Google’s own crawler documentation states plainly that Google-Extended governs specified AI training and grounding uses, things like feeding future Gemini models or grounding certain Vertex AI responses, and explicitly does not affect a site’s inclusion in Google Search or function as a ranking signal. Blocking it does not remove a publisher from AI Overviews, AI Mode, standard Top Stories, or Top Stories embedded inside an AI Overview. Shehata is right to keep hammering on this, because the confusion is not a fringe misunderstanding. It’s the default assumption across the industry.
Google began testing a generative AI exclusion inside Search Console in June, currently limited to a subset of UK site owners. It lets an eligible publisher exclude their links and content from AI Overviews, AI Mode, and generative Discover features specifically, without touching their eligibility for traditional Search. Google’s support documentation says an excluded site’s content won’t appear in those features and won’t even be used as an input for generating a response. Choose that setting and, by Shehata’s reading, you almost certainly lose your spot in the embedded Top Stories carousel too, since it’s just a collection of publisher links riding inside one of the covered surfaces.
Google has not confirmed what happens next at the layout level. Would the AI Overview keep showing an embedded carousel built from the publishers who remained opted in? Would Google fall back to a standalone Top Stories module instead? Nobody outside Mountain View knows yet, and Shehata is careful to label this a high-confidence interpretation rather than a documented outcome. That kind of restraint is rarer than it should be in AI SEO commentary right now, and it’s a large part of why I trust his data over the louder takes circulating on the same topic.
I think the bigger story here is not the mechanics of Google-Extended versus the Search Console control, even though publishers genuinely need to understand that difference before they touch a setting. The bigger story is that AI Overviews’ central problem has always been trust , not visibility. Users don’t yet have a reliable way to know whether an AI-generated answer is drawing on something a credible newsroom actually reported or synthesizing something thinner. Pulling Top Stories, with its named publishers, real bylines, and direct links, into the body of the AI Overview instead of stacking it below a wall of generated text is a genuine, if incomplete, answer to that problem. I’ve watched Google reshuffle where news lives in its results since the “vertical creep” days of 2006. This is the first move in the AI Overview era that looks aimed at rebuilding trust rather than just reducing clicks to the open web.
Although this is my considered opinion, it comes with a caveat. A step in the right direction is not the same as a finished solution, and Google’s refusal to document what happens to publishers who opt out is exactly the kind of ambiguity that erodes the trust this move is supposed to build.
For SEO practitioners managing news clients or in-house newsroom sites, three things are worth doing this week rather than waiting for Google to clarify the layout question.
First, separate your controls before you touch either one. Audit whether your site currently blocks Google-Extended, uses the new Search Console generative AI exclusion, or neither, and document which surfaces each one actually governs. Treating them as interchangeable is how a site accidentally forfeits AI Overview visibility while believing it only opted out of training data.
Second, if you have access to the Search Console exclusion , test it on a URL-prefix property or a single section before applying it sitewide. Google’s control supports inheritance between parent and child properties, which means a news publisher can trial the exclusion on, say, an opinion vertical and watch what happens to that section’s Top Stories eligibility before deciding whether the tradeoff is worth it domain-wide.
Third, start pulling Google’s generative AI performance reports in Search Console now , and pair them with a tool like NewzDash that tracks how often your URLs surface inside Top Stories carousels versus embedded AI Overview placements. You cannot make an informed opt-out decision without a baseline for how much visibility is actually at stake, and that baseline needs to exist before you flip the setting, not after.
Twenty years ago, “vertical creep” meant publishers had to figure out how a blended results page would treat their headlines. Today, it means figuring out how a generated answer treats them instead. The mechanism changed, but the need for publishers to understand exactly what they’re opting into, and out of, did not. John Shehata is doing the unglamorous work of documenting that shift in real time, and until Google says otherwise, his data is the closest thing the industry has to ground truth.
